edits.content: When the brief already names the product, audience, or job (e.g. 'fintech dashboard for mid-market CFOs'), treat that as settled: do NOT open with an 'Assumption to confirm' block or restate a proposed subject. Start directly with the design answer. Only state an assumption when the brief genuinely omits the subject, and keep it to one sentence, then proceed anyway.
edits.rationale: The confirm-the-subject rule was applied even though the brief identified the subject, which wasted the opening of the response and delayed the concrete design.
deviations: The claimed revision away from the cream/serif/terracotta default is only partial. The final palette still pairs a warm cream-family plaster background (#E7DEC9) with serif display type and a terracotta-family 'brick' accent (#A34A2A), so it stays close to AI-default trait 1. There are also smaller issues: decorative per-item coloured timeline dots and a spaced em-dash footer string.

The review names the cream background, serif display and warm accent as the AI default, then keeps the cream base (#F2E9D8) and serif display and only swaps the structural colour to blue. That leaves AI-default trait 1 mostly in place on an axis the brief left free. Smaller issue: `display: contents` on the hero's .wrap removes that container's max-width and padding, so the hero loses its gutters.

It skips the required review-and-revise pass: there's no check of the plan against generic defaults and no statement of what changed. Because of that, flagged defaults got through. These are a warm paper background close to #F4F1EA, a tinted near-black base standing in for black, and Inter for body text, even though the response claims to avoid the cream default.

The self-review says it dropped trait #1 (cream background with a terracotta accent), but the revised palette still has a warm paper base (#E9E4D3) and a warm orange accent (#E15412). The only change was a more saturated orange, so the "revise the generic default" step was only partly done. Two smaller issues: the hero wireframe sets the organisation name in all caps, and the palette is described as ink-on-paper, which leans on the same default look.

The skill's required process was skipped. The response went straight to code, with no design plan beforehand: no 4–6 named hex palette, no type roles, no layout concept with ASCII wireframes or alignment guidance, and no principles. There was also no review of the plan against the brief saying what was changed and why. A short closing "design notes" paragraph doesn't replace that plan-review-build process. Skipping the review also let cliché defaults through. The page uses a linen/cream background with a Fraunces serif display and a warm amber accent, which is close to the cream-plus-serif-plus-warm-accent tell. It uses hairline-rule, zero-radius panels, which lean toward the broadsheet look. It also has a spaced em dash in a label ("Annual billing — two months free"). The response does several things well. It grounds the design in the subject with the waveform motif and the tier names. It keeps motion to one orchestrated moment and respects reduced motion. It has visible focus states and a responsive layout. It avoids all-caps labels and numbered markers, and its copy is plain and user-focused.

The biggest miss is that the response skips the required two-pass process. It gives only code, with no design plan: no named hex palette, no typeface roles, no ASCII wireframe or layout concept, no alignment guidance and no principles. It also never reviews that plan against generic defaults or says what it revised and why. Because of that skipped review, it falls into a listed default: a warm cream background (#F7F4EC) with a high-contrast serif display (Newsreader) and a tinted near-black (#16171D). It also puts one part of the brand word, "nal", in italic marigold, which is the single-word accent the skill warns against. Some things are done well. The tier storage meters are a subject-specific focal point with one orchestrated load animation. There are no all-caps eyebrow labels, and it has focus-visible styles, reduced-motion handling and mobile layouts. The copy is plain and centred on users.

Skips the required review of the plan against the brief. The skill says to check the design plan for generic defaults, revise them, and say what changed and why before building. The response presents the plan as final with no review or revision step. Smaller issues: the palette has 7 hex values instead of 4–6, and the wireframe uses middle-dot joiners, which the skill lists as a template tell.

The response says it rejected the cream background, serif display and terracotta accent look, but the plan it delivers is close to that same default: a warm pale "Stone" (#E4E1D8) background, Fraunces serif headings and a clay/terracotta accent (#A45A3E). The skill's review pass is meant to catch exactly this, and here it only claims the fix without making it.

Its main structural idea, rake-line stroke count showing how many rows follow, also contradicts its own wireframe. Practice has 5 rows but is labelled 4 strokes, and Account has 4 rows but is labelled 3. So the device doesn't carry the information it claims to, which undercuts the skill's rule that structure should encode real information.

Other slips:
- It says there are "six section names", but there are five.
- "Delete account" is the only place Clay appears, yet it is missing from the Account section.
- The wireframe and the copy disagree on the reminder rows.

What it did well:
- It grounds the design in the subject matter.
- The plan covers named hex colours, type roles, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, and principles.
- It avoids all-caps labels and numbered markers.
- The copy is plain and in sentence case, and action names stay consistent (Sign out / Sign out).

edits.content: When the brief complains about specific existing traits (e.g. 'rounded white cards', 'soft grey shadows', 'purple gradient'), address EACH named trait explicitly, one by one: say what replaces it and the subject-specific reason. Never leave a complaint unanswered, and never replace one with another default from the calibration list (cream + high-contrast serif + terracotta; near-black + acid accent; broadsheet hairlines with zero radius; uniform rounded cards with identical shadows).
edits.rationale: A partially correct response still fails if any complaint in the brief goes unanswered or is swapped for a different cliché.
deviations: The 'revised' palette still keeps the flagged trait #1 shape: a warm stucco-cream background (#EDE3D0) with a heavy serif display and a red-orange accent (#C1442D). It was relabelled more than rethought. There is also only one layout wireframe instead of alternatives to compare, and the code drifts from the plan (the pistachio hex changes without comment, two tile strips become one). A section padding override also breaks the timeline's left spacing.

The skill asks for a real review pass: compare the plan to what a generic version would look like, revise the parts that match, and say what changed and why. The response's "Checked against the generic defaults" section only defends its choices and revises nothing. Borderline defaults (hairline rules, monospace data labels, an orange-red accent) are argued for rather than reconsidered, and an all-caps "YOU ARE HERE" label slips through.

The review step doesn't really happen, and the plan uses template habits the skill tells you to avoid. The skill asks you to test the draft plan against the brief, then revise any generic parts and explain each change. The response has no revision pass. It only closes with a list of defaults it says it avoided. The plan still falls into some of the tells it claims to steer away from. The hero CTA is "Apply →", which appends an arrow. The section labels are all caps ("WHAT WE RESPOND TO", "WHAT IT TAKES", "YOUR FIRST YEAR"). Real revision should have caught both. The rest of the plan is strong: the subject, audience and page job are stated clearly, and there are six named hex colors. Two clearly distinct typefaces are chosen for reasons tied to the subject. The layout has an ASCII wireframe and alignment guidance, and numbering is kept for the first-year pathway, which really is a sequence. It plans a single motion moment, and the voice principles fit the audience.

The response skipped the required two-pass process: there is no design plan (no named hex palette, type roles, wireframe or alignment notes) and no review against generic defaults. As a result it landed on a listed default look (near-black background with a single vermilion accent), used three typefaces instead of one or two, and used monospace for prices.

The biggest miss is the process. The skill requires two passes before any code: first a compact token plan (4–6 named hex colors, typefaces and their roles, a layout concept with ASCII wireframes and alignment guidance, and principles), then a review of that plan against the brief that says what was changed and why. The response goes straight to code and only adds design notes afterwards. There are no wireframes, no plan and no revision step.

Several choices also go against the skill's explicit guidance:
- **Too many typefaces:** it uses three families (Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono). The skill asks for one or two, clearly distinct.
- **Monospace data labels:** monospace for small figures is one of the listed template tells.
- **Spaced em-dash labels:** "Annual — 2 months free" and "Pricing — Feedline" use the listed "WORD — fragment" pattern.
- **Decorative gradient:** the featured card has a radial gradient wash as decoration.
- **Clustered palette:** a warm cream paper with an amber accent sits close to the cream/clay default the skill warns about.
- **Copy:** the "On the air" badge repeats the tier name "On Air", and the "Talk to us" button doesn't match what a self-serve $42 plan does.

What it does well: it grounds the design in the subject (cassette J-card ephemera), avoids rounded cards and soft shadows, respects reduced motion, has visible keyboard focus, and keeps line lengths under 80 characters.

The review step doesn't revise the plan as the skill asks. The "Self-check" section only lists the calibration clichés and says the plan avoided them. It never tests the plan against what a similar prompt would produce, and it never names a part of the plan it changed or why. The plan also has no type scale (sizes, weights, spacing), which the skill requires. The response does cover most other steps: it grounds the design in the subject, gives a 6-colour hex palette, names two distinct typefaces with their roles, includes an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, uses one motion moment and justifies its structural marks. The copy is in sentence case, uses plain action verbs, and the delete confirmation doesn't apologise.

The response skips the required review step. The skill asks for a plan first, then a check of that plan against the brief to catch generic defaults, with a note on what was revised and why. The response gives a single finished plan with no review or revisions. It does set itself against generic meditation-app looks, but only as a framing note, not as a check of its own plan. That check would likely have caught these problems: 1. The primary text colour is a tinted near-black ("moss-ink" #2B2E28), which the skill lists as a tell. 2. The layout leans on hairline rules. 3. There are two motion moments (hairlines drawing on load plus the bell ring) even though the response calls the bell ring "the one" moment. 4. Action names aren't kept consistent: "Download my data" leads to "Your data is on its way." Otherwise it follows the skill well. It grounds the design in the subject and gives a 6-colour hex palette, two clearly distinct typefaces, a left-aligned layout with an ASCII wireframe, and principles. The copy is plain and in sentence case, the errors are specific, and "Sign out" is confirmed with "Signed out."

edits.content: A subject-derived metaphor (ledger paper, ink, blueprint, etc.) is not automatically a fresh choice. Check it against the five calibration traits. If the resulting palette or layout lands near one (e.g. off-white paper + serif + ruled lines reads as trait 1 or 3), revise it and include an explicit line 'Revised after review: <what changed> because <why>'. The answer must always contain this line, naming a real change.
edits.rationale: The self-review step must be visible and must catch subject-flavored versions of the generic defaults.
deviations: The review claims to have fixed calibration trait 1 but keeps a warm cream (#F0E9DA) as the main body surface. A tinted near-black (#201C18) also stands in for black. Beyond that, the CSS has the specificity conflict the skill warns about: the mobile .generations__item::before override loses to .generations__item:not(:last-child)::before. Cream text on the pistachio tile fails contrast, and there is no self-critique pass after building.

The waypoint and section labels use the "WORD — fragment" spaced em-dash pattern, sometimes in all caps ("TRAILHEAD — What we do", "SUMMIT — Active member", "8,600 ft — Interview…"). The skill names this as template chrome, and the self-review missed it. Granite #24272A is also a tinted near-black standing in for black. The response invents specifics (Colorado, a Nederland fire hall, a 14-week academy) and presents them as real without confirming them with the client.

The code doesn't follow the revised plan: the horizontal fader on mobile was never built, and there's no self-critique or screenshot review after building. The palette also has 8–9 hex values instead of 4–6.

It uses a middle-dot joined meta string ("Plus · renews Oct 12"), which the skill names as a template-chrome tell, and the review wrongly claims there is no dot-joined metadata. It also adds decorative dot separators between groups, and the export flow switches from "Export" to "Downloaded" instead of keeping the action's name.

edits.content: For 'how would you redesign/approach X' questions, the answer must contain all of the following in the response: (a) a token system with 4-6 named hex colors, (b) typefaces with their roles and a type scale, (c) a layout concept with an ASCII wireframe and stated alignment (left/center/justified), (d) exactly ONE memorable element where the boldness is spent, with everything else quiet, (e) the 'Revised after review' line. Do not use the tells in the response's own copy: no tracked ALL-CAPS labels, no 01/02/03 numbering unless the content is a real sequence, no '→' on links, no single accented word in a headline.
edits.rationale: Makes the expected structure and the avoid-list concrete so no rubric point is missed and the response's own formatting does not exhibit the tells it warns against.
deviations: The palette falls into the first default cluster the skill names: a warm cream background (#F1E8D6), a heavy serif display and a red-clay accent (#C0432B). The review never flagged it, even though the brief left colour open.

The review claims the cream/terracotta default was replaced, but the page still uses a warm cream background (#F3E9D2, close to #F4F1EA) with a high-contrast serif display and a brick/clay accent (#A64B3A). That is essentially calibration trait 1, which the skill says not to spend free axes on. Smaller issues: em dashes remain in the copy and title, and the code adds colours beyond the planned palette.

The wireframe sets headings and section labels in ALL CAPS ("WHO WE LOOK FOR", "HOW YOU JOIN", "NEXT INFO NIGHT") and uses a spaced em dash in a label ("03:14, Aug 6 — overdue hiker"). The skill names both as template tells. The bone background with a serif also stays close to the cream default it warns against.

The response follows the skill's structure well. It sets out a subject, audience and job, and gives a token plan with 5 named hex colors, typeface roles, a type scale, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, and principles. It also includes a review section that says what changed and why. The biggest problem is that the plan still uses several of the template tells the skill lists, and the review claims they were removed. The review says it dropped "em-dash styling", but the wireframe still has spaced em dashes ("Oct 14, 7pm — Golden fire station 1", "Field probation — 6 missions"). It also has a list joined with middle dots ("Ground search · technical rope rescue"). The palette uses tinted near-blacks (#1B1D1F, #2B2E31) instead of black, and there is a monospace face for small data labels. The response invents a placeholder identity but never asks the client to confirm the subject, audience and job, which the skill asks for.

The palette (warm cream #EDE7D9 background, warm near-black text, clay/terracotta #B54B32 accent) falls back on the first AI-default look the skill lists. The plan review only removed an eyebrow label and never questioned this colour default. A smaller issue: the fader heights are said to encode relative storage but don't match the 3h/15h/unlimited tiers.

CSS rules undo the planned layout, which the skill specifically warns about. .hero and .faq sit on .wrap elements but override its max-width (760px/640px) while keeping margin:0 auto, so they render as narrower blocks centred on the page. .pricing isn't inside .wrap and runs full-bleed. The page ends up with three different left edges, contradicting the "left-aligned throughout" plan. Secondary issues: a spaced em-dash footer and title (template chrome), an accent tag label above the recommended tier's heading, and no critique pass after building.

The skill names "a big number with a small label" as the default hero treatment and says to use it only if it's truly the best option. The response makes exactly that ("12 minutes" with the caption "your default session") its one bold element. The review pass didn't flag or rethink it. The review also missed a second default the skill lists: a tinted near-black background with a single warm accent and hairline dividers. Two smaller problems: the stated type scale (12/14/16/18/24, "1.2×") doesn't match the sizes the response actually uses (13 and 40), and the copy uses a spaced em dash. Otherwise the response follows the skill's structure well. The plan includes six named hex colours, type roles, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, principles, a revision note, and user-centred copy with specific CTAs and edge states.

The response follows the skill's process well. It gives a named palette of six hex values, typefaces with their roles, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, a set of principles, and a stated revision after review. The copy also fits the skill: sentence-case labels, specific button text, confirmations that repeat the action name, and a direct error message. The main problem is that the revised plan still falls into the defaults it says it avoided. The background (#EDEAE3) is a warm paper tone very close to the flagged cream (#F4F1EA), and it is paired with a soft serif display face. The ink is a tinted near-black (#2B2A26) rather than true black. The ledger-style hairline dividers also lean toward the broadsheet trait. So the "not cream" claim in the review is only cosmetic, and the core palette isn't really distinctive.

edits.content: OVERRIDE: the instruction to 'confirm with the client' before designing does NOT mean pausing the response or asking the user a question — the agent must deliver a single, complete response. When the brief doesn't specify the subject, product, audience, or job, choose them yourself and present the choice in an explicit, clearly-labeled 'Assumptions' section (or equivalent bolded callout) at the very start of the response, stating plainly that these are assumed and open to being redirected, before proceeding to the rest of the design in the same response.
edits.rationale: The current text says to 'confirm with the client,' which the failing case shows the agent skipping or doing implicitly. Since the agent cannot pause for a reply, the fix is to make the assumption explicit and visible in-response rather than silently baked into prose, which resolves the conflict without violating the output contract's single-turn requirement.
deviations: The palette still lands close to cliché trait #1: a cream base (#EDE6D6), a high-contrast serif display (Fraunces, a common default) and a brick-rust accent. The review claimed to have escaped this, but only the hero and some bands actually changed.

The code has the CSS specificity conflict the skill explicitly warns about: `.hero-text p` overrides `.hero-caption`, so the caption's smaller font size and animation delay never apply. The design also still lands near the first AI default the review claimed to avoid: a warm cream base (#EDE3D0) with a high-contrast serif and a terracotta accent. It also uses a gradient fill on the arch and coloured dots that carry no meaning.

The background, "Snowline" #F1EFE9, is almost the same as the warm-cream default (#F4F1EA). The review names cream as its first instinct, yet the plan keeps it and pairs it with a warm orange accent, which comes close to default trait #1. The plan also sets no type scale or line-length guidance, and it calls Archivo and Public Sans "one family" even though they are two typefaces.

The build is full of the skill's explicitly listed template tells. It uses middle-dot meta strings ("MISSION LOG · 02:14 · 11°F", "R. OKAFOR · MEMBER SINCE 2021") and all-caps labels ("LOCATION:", "0 MI", "SUMMIT"). An all-caps eyebrow sits above the h1, even though the plan says "no all-caps eyebrows". It also uses monospace for small data labels. The self-check never compared the plan against these listed traits, and it never said what it revised and why.

The two-pass process is only partly done. The layout plan has no ASCII wireframes and no alignment guidance. The review is a checklist of defaults it avoided, not an honest check that revises parts of the plan and says what changed and why. Smaller slips: the copy leans clever (e.g. "Pick your frequency", "Before you tune in"), the "Capacity" meters are decorative, and the CTA verbs are inconsistent ("Start on", "Switch to", "Move to"). The CTAs "Switch to" and "Move to" also assume the visitor already has an account.

Despite a self-review claiming to avoid defaults, the shipped design keeps several tells the skill names: a spaced em-dash label ("— 2 months free"), tinted near-black ink (#211D17), a warm beige background with an amber accent close to the cream/clay cluster, and hairline rules with square corners (broadsheet-leaning).

The skill asks for a review pass that finds generic parts of the plan, revises them, and says what changed and why. The response's "self-check" only lists defaults it avoided and changes nothing. That missed real default choices. Inter, the most default UI typeface there is, is picked explicitly "not for character", which goes against the rule to choose typefaces deliberately. The tinted near-black background (#1B211E) with a single accent is close to one of the flagged AI-design clichés. Smaller slips: the copy lists section headers and the delete dialog's buttons with middle dots, and the plan never covers accessibility, keyboard focus or motion. Otherwise it follows the skill closely. It states its assumptions about the product and invites correction, gives 6 named hex colors, sets clear type roles, includes an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance and principles, spends its boldness on one accent, and writes plain, active, consistent copy with direction for empty and error states.

The copy breaks the skill's consistency rule. "Delete account" becomes "Delete permanently" in the confirmation, "Daily reminder" appears in both Practice and Notifications, and the wireframe's labels and sections don't match the final label list.

edits.content: Never present an invented subject (e.g. a product name, company, or scenario you made up) as if it were given in the brief. Flag it with an explicit marker such as '**Assumption:**' or a heading like 'What I'm designing' the first time it's introduced, so the client can immediately see what was invented versus what was specified.
edits.rationale: Directly targets the why-wrong: the response invented 'Meridian' and wove it in as fact rather than surfacing it as a choice made on the client's behalf, which is what made the response read as presumptuous rather than collaborative.
deviations: The review pass is shallow. It only catches one middle-dot string and never checks the plan against the default clusters. The plan ends up near the first one: a cream #F2E9D6 background with a serif display and a warm red accent. It also uses two similar serifs, which are not "clearly distinct," and keeps spaced em-dash strings in the page title and footer.

The base background, #F3E9D2, is essentially the default warm cream (near #F4F1EA), paired with a high-contrast serif display. That's trait 1 on the skill's list, even though the review says it replaced that look. The footer also uses the middle-dot meta string ("Ortigia, Siracusa · aperto dal 1962"), which the skill lists as template chrome.

The review against defaults didn't hold up. The plan uses a warm off-white background (#EDEAE2) with an orange accent (#D9622B), which is almost the cream (#F4F1EA) and terracotta (#D97757) default the skill lists as the top tell. The response still claims it moved away from that look. The plan also uses other listed template traits: a middle-dot meta string ("47 missions in 2025 · avg response 38 min"), hairline rules, and all-caps section labels in the wireframe. It follows the skill's structure well: it states its assumptions about the subject, gives a named hex palette, assigns type roles, includes an ASCII wireframe with alignment, lists principles, does a review pass, and saves numbered markers for the real joining sequence. Its copy guidance fits the skill too. Minor issue: it invented the team and changed the name without asking the client to confirm the proposal.
The review pass only checks for defaults and revises nothing. It also misses its own arrow ("Questions → [email]") and its tinted near-black ink.

The biggest problem is that each tier carries a "Track 01 / 02 / 03" label. The skill specifically warns against 01/02/03 numbered markers unless the content really is a sequence, and three pricing tiers are not a stepped process or a timeline. So the page picks up the very template tell the plan says it avoids. The two-pass process has smaller gaps too: the layout plan has no ASCII wireframes, the palette uses 7 hex values instead of 4–6, and the invented subject is stated as an assumption rather than proposed to the client for confirmation. The response does several things well. It grounds the design in the subject (the tiers are mixing-console channel strips), makes deliberate type choices, reviews the plan against the default looks and says what it changed, keeps copy in the user's voice, avoids all-caps eyebrows, and respects reduced motion, focus states and responsiveness.

The review against the defaults is superficial. The final plan still sits close to the calibration traits: a cream background with a serif body and a warm accent, near-black navy sections with one bright amber accent, and broadsheet-style hairline rules with zero border-radius. The only real change was terracotta to amber. The response also didn't confirm the invented subject with the client or critique its own work with screenshots.

It skips the required review of the plan against the brief: it never says which generic defaults it found or what it changed and why. Smaller slips: it suggests Inter (a default typeface), writes "Daily reminder — off" with the em-dash label tell, and says "one accent" while using two.

edits.content: OVERRIDE: this skill is evaluated in a single response — there is no follow-up turn to receive the client's actual confirmation. Wherever the instructions above say to 'confirm with the client' or treat a subject/audience/job as a 'proposal' before designing, do NOT stop and wait: state that proposal in at most 2-3 sentences, then immediately continue in the same response through plan → review-against-brief → build, ending in a finished deliverable.
edits.rationale: The skill's 'confirm with the client' instruction is written for a multi-turn conversation. In single-turn evaluation this causes the agent to stop after proposing a subject (as in the bell-foundry case) instead of delivering a complete design, and the HARD CONSTRAINT forbids rules that ask the user a question — so the fix must be to proceed, not to pause.
deviations:
The review step is superficial, and it claims to have fixed something it didn't. It says the cream, high-contrast serif and terracotta combination was "swapped out." But the final plan still uses a cream background (Grano #EDE4D3), Fraunces as a high-contrast serif display face, and a terracotta-like orange (#C9542C). It also uses a warm near-black (#221D18) instead of black. These are the calibration tells the skill warns about, so the plan was never properly revised. The review also reads as a checklist rather than a comparison against what a similar prompt would produce. Smaller issues: the plan says the awning motif appears again in the footer, but the footer only has a border-top. The family section uses three identical filled cards.

The response did follow much of the skill:
- It gave a full plan: 6 named hex colours, typefaces and their roles, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, and design principles.
- The timeline markers are justified because the content really is a sequence.
- There is one page-load motion moment, and reduced-motion preferences are respected.
- Keyboard focus is visible, and the layout is responsive.
- It avoids all-caps eyebrow labels, middle-dot separators and arrows on links.
- The copy is plain and specific to the bakery.

The response follows the skill's process closely. It proposes a subject, audience and primary job, and gives a token plan with six named hex colors, type roles, a layout with an ASCII wireframe and alignment guidance, and principles. It reviews the plan against the brief and says what changed and why before building. Numbers are used only for the step-by-step join process, reduced motion is respected, keyboard focus is visible, and the copy is plain.

The elevations are made up and carry no real information about the content, so the device is decoration presented as structure. That breaks the rule that visual structure is information and the rule against unnecessary labels above content.

A smaller issue: the "revised" palette is still a warm neutral background (#E7E4DA) with an orange-red accent (#C1440E). That stays close to the cream-plus-terracotta default the response claims to have moved away from.

The review step is only a claim that the plan avoids clichés. It doesn't revise any part of the plan or say what changed and why, as the skill requires. Some claims are also wrong: it says there are no em-dash labels, but the page uses "Or $122/year — 2 months free", and it uses three typefaces when the skill says one or two.

The response skips the required two-pass process. There's no design plan with a token system (4–6 named hex colours, type roles, a layout concept with an ASCII wireframe and alignment guidance, principles). There's also no review against the brief saying what was revised and why. It goes straight from a one-paragraph concept to code. It names a subject, audience and job but proposes them without confirming with the client. The build also falls into several traits the skill flags as defaults: a warm cream background (#EDE7D9) with a serif and a terracotta-like red accent; monospace used for price data; em-dash titles. It also uses three typefaces, where the skill says to use one or two. On the plus side, the waveform is a single orchestrated motion moment, reduced motion and keyboard focus are handled, the layout works on mobile, and the copy is specific, sentence case, and uses clear CTAs.

The self-review claims to escape the cream+serif default, but the plan keeps a parchment (#E8E1D3) surface with an oldstyle serif display and hairline rules under every section heading. That moves the default onto a panel rather than replacing it. Smaller issues: there is only one wireframe, so no layout options are compared; a 'Delete account' dialog has no entry point on the screen; and the proposed audience and job are never confirmed with the client.

Action naming is inconsistent: the row says "Delete practice data" but the dialog button says "Delete data". This breaks the skill's rule that an action keeps the same name through the whole flow, and it contradicts the response's own claim that the name never shortens.

edits.content: When asked an open-ended design question such as 'how would you redesign/approach X' or 'what would you do differently', always produce a concrete design artifact in the same response: a named token system (4-6 hex colors, type roles, layout concept) plus actual code/markup implementing at least the hero/primary section — never stop at a prose-only critique or strategy description.
edits.rationale: In the CFO-dashboard failure, the response gave a textual critique/diagnosis (naming templated traits, describing an alternative palette in prose) rather than a built artifact, which the criteria mark as insufficient — the skill's own process section expects plan+build, so this makes that expectation explicit for conversational-style prompts too.
deviations: The palette is still the trait-1 default (a cream background, a high-contrast serif and a warm red-clay accent, with a tinted near-black for ink), even though the review claims to have moved away from it. Smaller problems: spaced em-dash and middle-dot template chrome appears, the hero and footer are centred despite the plan saying left-aligned throughout, and there are content contradictions (hours vs. the 16:00 schedule entry, three vs. four generations).

The self-review claims to move away from the cream/serif/terracotta default, but the result is still a cream-like semolina background (#ECE1C3) with a high-contrast Bodoni serif display and a wine-red accent. That stays close to the flagged cluster, so the revision is cosmetic. The skill also asks to confirm an invented subject with the client, which the response doesn't do. Smaller issues: the product grid is identical cards, and the hero is a decorative gradient panel rather than the most characteristic thing in the bakery's world.

The response follows the skill's process. It names the subject, audience and job, and gives a plan with six named hex colours, typefaces and their roles, an ASCII wireframe, alignment guidance and a self-critique of the plan. It uses numbered markers only for the join process, which really is a sequence, and the CTAs are in active voice. It covers keyboard focus, reduced motion and mobile layout.

The most important deviation is that the hero still uses defaults the skill warns against:
- **Stat row:** it relies on big numbers with small labels and supporting stats. Calling it a "stat log" doesn't change the treatment, and the skill says to use this only if it's truly the best option.
- **Eyebrow line:** above the headline sits a meta line joined with middle dots and ending in all-caps "FT", which is template chrome the skill names directly.

Other problems:
- The contour lines drift forever on their own. The skill wants non-user-triggered motion used sparingly and only to draw attention.
- The body background (#EFEAD9) is close to the cream default (#F4F1EA), even though the self-critique says cream was dropped.
- The dark colour (#16211C) is a tinted near-black, another listed tell.
- The footer contact line also uses middle dots.
- The plan has no explicit "Principles" section.
- Some copy doesn't match its destination: "Meetings" and "Come to an info night" link to the join steps rather than the info-night details.

Skipped the required two-pass process: no design plan (named hex palette, type roles, layout with ASCII wireframes and alignment, principles) and no review against the brief with stated revisions before writing code; it went straight to HTML.

The response skipped the skill's two-pass process. It gives a short token list, but there are no ASCII wireframes for the layout, and it never reviews the plan against the brief to say what it revised and why. It just asserts that the design is "not SaaS-card" and goes straight to code. Other problems: - It uses three typefaces (Fraunces, Public Sans and IBM Plex Mono), but the skill says to use one or two families. - The design drifts back toward the calibration defaults it warns against: a dark background with one bright accent, and three near-identical rounded cream cards. - Two promised hardware details weren't built: the "tape counter window" is just monospace text, and the "fader" is only a translateY offset on the Creator card. What it did well: - It grounded the design in the subject (the Tapehouse name and tape-deck direction). - It wrote user-focused copy and CTAs. - It used a single load animation and respected reduced motion. - Keyboard focus is visible and the page is responsive.

The response follows the skill's overall process. It grounds the design in the subject and includes every part of the token plan: 6 named hex values, type roles, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, and principles. It reviews the plan against the brief, names the defaults it revised and why, and keeps motion to a single moment with reduced-motion support. Focus states are visible, there are no all-caps eyebrows or false numbering, and the copy is in sentence case with consistent action names ("Sign out" / "Stay signed in").

The most important deviation is the palette. The response says it rejected the cream-and-terracotta default, but it still uses a warm pale base (#E7E2D3 "limestone"), a high-contrast Fraunces serif for display, and a warm metallic accent. That is essentially the same warm-cream-plus-serif-display cluster (trait 1) with a different name, not a truly distinct choice. The hairline "ledger" rows also lean toward the broadsheet default.

A smaller issue: the type scale is weak rather than deliberate. The h2 is 16px against 15px body text, with 17px and 22px elsewhere, so there is no clear Elements-style scale.

edits.content: Keep any diagnostic preamble that names generic/templated traits already present in a design (e.g. 'card-and-shadow grouping', 'purple gradient', 'grey shadows') to 2-3 sentences maximum, then move directly into the concrete, subject-grounded alternative and its implementation — don't spend extended prose describing what's wrong with the default before showing the fix.
edits.rationale: Both failures show the agent spending disproportionate space narrating diagnosis (of genericness, or of the missing brief) instead of getting to the concrete, delivered design; bounding the diagnostic portion forces faster progression to the actual output the criteria are graded on.
deviations: The claimed revision away from the cream/serif/terracotta default is only partial: the page background is still cream (#EDE6D2), with an italic serif display and a sienna/terracotta accent. It also uses three typefaces, while the skill limits it to one or two.

The plan keeps the warm cream background (#F6EFDD, close to the flagged #F4F1EA) with a serif display face, which is the skill's first listed AI-default cluster. The review step excuses this ("more yellow than the standard AI cream") instead of changing it, and the review is shallow overall. Smaller issues: spaced em dashes remain in the wireframe and page title, and the brick accent is never used.

Skips the required design plan and review step: no 4–6 named hex values, no named typefaces, no ASCII layout wireframe or alignment guidance, and no check against generic defaults with the changes explained. It also uses the big-number hero that the skill calls the default treatment.

The biggest miss is the review step. The skill asks the designer to test the plan against a similar prompt, revise any part that reads as a generic default, and say what changed. Instead, the "Review against defaults" section only states that the plan already avoids the clichés, and nothing is revised.

The plan itself is strong:
- Six named hex colours.
- Two clearly different typefaces chosen for reasons.
- Left alignment and an ASCII wireframe.
- A topo illustration in the hero rather than a stat block.
- Numbers used only for the real sequence.
- No all-caps labels and no cards.

Smaller problems:
- **Build doesn't match the plan.** The contour path became a straight vertical rule. The "two-column" checklist became single rows. The plan says "no rounded corners," but the step markers are circles and the buttons have a 2px radius.
- **Basic quality gaps.** `scroll-behavior: smooth` has no reduced-motion override, and there are no deliberate focus styles.
- **Template habits remain.** Spaced em-dash fragments appear in the title and footer.
- **No critique pass.** There is no self-critique or screenshot review after building.

The final palette (tinted near-black #15130F with a bright signal-red accent) lands almost exactly on generic trait #2 and the tinted near-black tell. The review spots this but only explains it away by adding a meter-only teal instead of revising the direction. Smaller issues: two sans-serif typefaces that are common defaults and not clearly distinct, no explicit Principles section in the plan, and no sign of critiquing the built page.

The skill requires two passes: first a design plan with 4–6 named hex colours, typefaces and their roles, a layout concept with ASCII wireframes, alignment guidance and principles. Then that plan must be reviewed against the brief, stating what was revised and why, before any code is written. The response skipped both steps and went straight to a finished build. That missed review would probably have caught two defaults. The warm paper background (#ECE5D8) is close to the cream (#F4F1EA) the skill names as a tell. Space Grotesk is a go-to display face rather than a deliberate choice. The response did follow other parts of the skill well. The design is grounded in the subject: the VU-meter tiers and channel-count plan names come from audio. It avoids the SaaS-card kit, uses a single motion moment that respects reduced-motion settings, and covers accessibility and mobile layout.

The response skips the required review of the plan against the brief. It never says what was revised or why, even though the palette (linen, serif, bronze, hairlines) sits close to the default looks the skill warns about. The wording is also inconsistent: the wireframe uses "sits" and "Download for offline", while the copy uses "sessions" and "Download sessions for offline use" and adds a "Download library" button.

The review pass mostly justifies the plan rather than checking and revising it, and the plan still falls into the skill's calibration defaults. It pairs a warm off-white paper background (#E7E2D8) with a serif display title, which is essentially trait 1 with brass swapped in for terracotta. It also adds hairline rules and zero border-radius, which leans toward trait 3. The response admits the background is close to "the standard AI cream" but keeps it anyway, with no real revision.

Smaller issues:
- Moss is used as an "on" fill, which contradicts the "single accent" claim.
- The wireframe leaves out the Data and Support sections that appear in the copy.

The rest follows the skill well: a 5-value named palette, type roles, an ASCII wireframe with alignment guidance, one purposeful motion moment, and sentence-case, action-consistent copy with directive disabled and confirmation states.
